questions.question:
D0 — Add gstack skill routing rules to CLAUDE.md?
Project/branch/task: plan-count-W42Czh on main, reviewing the Stripe payment webhook plan.
ELI10: gstack works best when your project's CLAUDE.md includes skill routing rules, so that requests like "review this diff" automatically reach the right skill. This is a one-time setup prompt per project. Note: plan mode is active, so if you pick A the CLAUDE.md edit and commit happen after the review, once plan mode exits.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Low either way; skills still work when invoked manually.
Recommendation: A because routing rules make skill invocation automatic with no downside.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: convenience of auto-routing versus keeping CLAUDE.md untouched.

options.label: Add routing rules (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Requests auto-route to the right gstack skill without typing slash commands. ✅ Teammates get the same routing since CLAUDE.md is committed. ❌ Adds a section to CLAUDE.md and a commit after plan mode exits.

options.label: No thanks, manual
options.description: ✅ CLAUDE.md stays exactly as it is in this fixture repo. ✅ Skills remain fully usable via explicit /skill-name invocation. ❌ You must remember which skill to call for each task.

questions.question:
D1 — Enable cross-project learnings search?
Project/branch/task: plan-count-W42Czh on main, Stripe webhook plan review.
ELI10: gstack can search learnings saved from your other projects on this machine to spot patterns that apply here. Everything stays local; no data leaves the machine. Good for solo developers; skip if you work across client codebases where cross-contamination matters.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Low. Either way, this project's own learnings still get searched.
Recommendation: A because local-only pattern reuse compounds review quality with no privacy cost for a single developer.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: broader pattern recall versus strict per-project isolation.

options.label: Enable cross-project (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Past learnings from any local project inform this and future reviews. ✅ Stays entirely on this machine, nothing is uploaded. ❌ Learnings from unrelated client codebases could surface where they do not apply.

options.label: Project-scoped only
options.description: ✅ Strict isolation; only this repo's learnings are ever consulted. ✅ Safe default for consultants juggling multiple client codebases. ❌ Loses cross-pollination of pitfalls already solved elsewhere.

questions.question:
D2 — Which implementation structure should the handler use?
Project/branch/task: main, Stripe payment webhook plan (HOLD SCOPE review).
ELI10: The plan adds a new StripePaymentWebhookHandler class but says it bypasses the existing WebhookDispatcher for a "clean namespace." The plan also says the handler runs inside the existing signature, dedup, and lock guards. If those guards live in or behind the dispatcher, bypassing it silently drops them. The structural question is where the new class plugs in.
Stakes if we pick wrong: A second routing path can lose dedup or locking on real payments, or drift when the guards change; nobody notices until a duplicate or unlocked update lands.
Recommendation: B because it achieves the dedicated-class goal while reusing the existing routing and guards by construction, with the smallest correct diff and no speculative service layer.
Completeness: A=4/10, B=8/10, C=9/10
Net: literal plan text with a parallel entry point, versus one dispatcher-routed class, versus that plus a service split that pays off only once a second payment event exists.

options.label: B) Register in WebhookDispatcher (recommended)
options.description: Completeness 8/10. (human: ~2h / CC: ~15min) ✅ Guard chain (signature, dedup, per-user lock, ownership) wraps the handler automatically. ✅ One routing table to read; handler testable through the dispatcher's existing test harness. ❌ Handler owns lookup/update/notify, so unit tests need a DB fixture or repository double.

options.label: A) Standalone handler, as written
options.description: Completeness 4/10. (human: ~1h / CC: ~10min) ✅ Fewest files touched; matches the current plan text literally. ✅ No change to WebhookDispatcher registration. ❌ Two routing paths for Stripe events; must independently prove every guard still wraps it and re-prove on every guard change.

options.label: C) Dispatcher + PaymentSuccessService
options.description: Completeness 9/10. (human: ~4h / CC: ~25min) ✅ Domain logic unit-testable without HTTP or the dispatcher. ✅ Ready-made seam for a second payment event type later. ❌ Second new class for one event type today, a premature abstraction until a second consumer exists.

questions.question:
D3 — What is the per-order fetch in the handler for?
Project/branch/task: main, Stripe payment webhook plan (HOLD SCOPE).
ELI10: The Performance section says each webhook looks up the user, then fetches each order in a loop, but nothing in the plan says what the orders are used for. The implementer will have to guess, and the guess decides whether this is a read for the email, a write that must sit inside the payment transaction, or dead work. I cannot see your domain, so this is your call.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Orders that should be marked paid stay unpaid, or the handler does N extra queries per webhook for nothing and slows toward Stripe's 10-second timeout.
Recommendation: A because the notification email is the only other consumer of user data in the plan, and a read-only batch is the least risky interpretation; correct me if orders must change state.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: read-for-email versus write-in-transaction versus no consumer at all.

options.label: A) Orders feed the email (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Read-only; one batched SELECT by user_id, no transactional coupling with the payment update. ✅ Failure of the read can share the notification rescue path without affecting payment state. ❌ If orders also need a status change, that write is silently missing.

options.label: B) Orders must be marked paid too
options.description: ✅ Order state stays consistent with the user payment status in one transaction. ✅ Single batched UPDATE ... WHERE user_id = ? AND payment_intent_id = ? under the existing lock. ❌ Widens the transaction and the idempotency surface; must define which orders belong to this PaymentIntent.

options.label: C) No consumer, drop the loop
options.description: ✅ Removes N queries per webhook and the whole N+1 finding. ✅ Smallest handler; nothing to test for orders. ❌ If a downstream feature relied on this fetch, it disappears without a trace.

questions.question:
1A — Should the notification email be sent only after the user update commits?
Project/branch/task: main, Stripe payment webhook plan (HOLD SCOPE), Section 1 Architecture.
ELI10: The plan says the user update and the email both happen inline, but not in which order relative to the database commit. If the email goes out while the transaction is still open and the commit then fails, the customer gets a "you're paid" email for a payment we did not record, and Stripe's retry sends a second one. Sequencing the send after the commit means the email only ever describes committed state.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Phantom confirmation emails and duplicate emails on retry, discovered by customers before on-call.
Recommendation: A because "explicit over clever" applies: make the order commit, then read orders, then send, and assert that order in a test.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10
Net: a fixed, tested ordering versus leaving the ordering to the implementer.

options.label: A) Commit first, then email (recommended)
options.description: Completeness 10/10. (human: ~30min / CC: ~5min) ✅ Email content always reflects committed payment state; a failed commit sends nothing. ✅ Test asserts the mail client is not invoked when the update raises before commit. ❌ Adds one explicit ordering constraint the handler comment must document.

options.label: B) Leave ordering unspecified
options.description: Completeness 3/10. (human: 0 / CC: 0) ✅ No change to the plan text. ✅ Implementer keeps freedom to structure the method. ❌ A phantom confirmation email on commit failure becomes possible and untested.

questions.question:
2A — How should the handler treat a failure on the email leg after the payment is committed?
Project/branch/task: main, Stripe payment webhook plan (HOLD SCOPE), Section 2 Error map.
ELI10: Today the plan has no error handling on the email. Any mail provider hiccup becomes a 500, and Stripe redelivers the whole payment event for up to 72 hours. The payment is already saved, so each redelivery is a blind replay that your own runbook forbids, plus another email attempt. The mail client already reports failures to a dashboard and alert, and the runbook already retries only the notification. The handler just needs to let that machinery work instead of fighting it.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Payment replays on every mail blip, alert storms, duplicate emails, and on-call unable to tell a failed payment from a failed email.
Recommendation: A because it names each exception, keeps the failure visible through the existing alert and traces, and matches the runbook's "retry only the notification" rule.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Net: named rescue with structured warning versus retry-then-rescue in the request path versus leaving the 500.

options.label: A) Rescue named mail errors, warn, return 200 (recommended)
options.description: Completeness 10/10. (human: ~1h / CC: ~10min) ✅ Rescues MailDeliveryError, MailTimeoutError, MailRateLimited, MailRenderError and the post-commit orders-read error by name; logs one structured warning with event_id, user_id, payment_intent_id, exception class. ✅ Event completes; failure visible via mail failure-rate alert and outcome trace; test asserts user paid + 200 + warning when mail raises. ❌ Notification retry stays manual through the existing runbook procedure.

options.label: B) Retry email once inline, then rescue
options.description: Completeness 6/10. (human: ~1.5h / CC: ~15min) ✅ Transient provider blips self-heal without on-call. ✅ Same named rescue and warning as A on the second failure. ❌ Adds mail latency twice inside Stripe's ~10s response budget and duplicates the mail client's own retry semantics if it has them.

options.label: C) Keep the plan: no handling, propagate
options.description: Completeness 2/10. (human: 0 / CC: 0) ✅ No new code in the handler. ✅ Stripe retries do eventually resend the email. ❌ Every retry replays a committed payment, violating the runbook; alert storms; duplicate emails.

answers: A) Rescue named mail errors, warn, return 200 (recommended)

questions.question:
3A — How should the handler look up the user from params.userId?
Project/branch/task: main, Stripe payment webhook plan (HOLD SCOPE), Section 3 Security.
ELI10: The plan pastes the user ID string straight into a SQL fragment. Your own contract says that string arrives unsanitized, may contain punctuation and Unicode, and that a valid Stripe signature does not make it SQL-safe. A customer whose ID contains an apostrophe breaks the query, gets a 500, and Stripe retries the same broken event for 72 hours while alerts fire. A hostile value in PaymentIntent metadata does worse. Bound parameters make the string data, never code.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Arbitrary SQL against the users table in the worst case, and a guaranteed poison-event alert loop for ordinary IDs in the common case.
Recommendation: A because parameterized queries through the existing DB client are the tried-and-true fix, cost a few lines, and the follow-on queries keyed by the internal primary key close the orders-scoping threat too.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=1/10
Net: bound parameter plus internal-key follow-ons versus escaping the string versus the plan as written.

options.label: A) Bound parameter via existing DB client (recommended)
options.description: Completeness 10/10. (human: ~1h / CC: ~10min) ✅ userId is passed as a bound value; update and orders read use the looked-up internal primary key. ✅ Tests cover O'Brien, SQL-metacharacter, Unicode, 255-char, and missing IDs with zero DB errors; a DB error here still propagates to 500 as retained. ❌ Requires the DB client to expose a parameterized lookup helper, or adding one small one.

options.label: B) Escape/quote the string before interpolating
options.description: Completeness 5/10. (human: ~30min / CC: ~5min) ✅ Blocks the obvious apostrophe breakage. ✅ Keeps the raw-fragment shape the plan describes. ❌ Escaping is driver- and encoding-specific; Unicode and multibyte edge cases have a history of bypasses, and it still deviates from the existing client pattern.

options.label: C) Keep raw SQL fragment as written
options.description: Completeness 1/10. (human: 0 / CC: 0) ✅ No change to the plan text. ✅ Nothing new to review. ❌ Injection vector plus a deterministic 72-hour poison-event loop for any ID containing a quote.

answers: A) Bound parameter via existing DB client (recommended)

questions.question:
4A — Should the handler suppress the email when the user row already carries this PaymentIntent?
Project/branch/task: main, Stripe payment webhook plan (HOLD SCOPE), Section 4 async ordering.
ELI10: The dedup guard only skips deliveries whose completion marker was written. If the email goes out and then the marker write fails, Stripe retries, the guard sees no marker, and the handler runs again. The user update is idempotent so the row is fine, but the customer gets a second "you're paid" email. The lookup already returns the row, so the handler can see that this PaymentIntent was recorded before and skip the send, using data that already exists.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Duplicate confirmation emails on every bookkeeping hiccup, and support tickets asking whether they were charged twice.
Recommendation: A because it closes the only remaining duplicate-email schedule with zero new storage, and logs the suppression so on-call can see it happened.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=2/10
Net: reuse the row as the sent-signal versus a mail-provider idempotency key versus accepting duplicates.

options.label: A) Skip email if row already has this PI (recommended)
options.description: Completeness 10/10. (human: ~45min / CC: ~10min) ✅ Lookup result already exposes payment_status and payment_intent_id; no new table or marker. ✅ Structured info log on suppression with event_id and payment_intent_id; test asserts exactly one mail call across two runs with the marker absent. ❌ A row that was already paid by the same PI before this handler ever ran also suppresses the email, which is the correct behavior but worth a comment.

options.label: B) Pass payment_intent_id as mail idempotency key
options.description: Completeness 7/10. (human: ~1h / CC: ~10min) ✅ Provider-side dedup even if two handler runs both attempt the send. ✅ No handler branching on row state. ❌ Depends on the shared mail client and provider supporting idempotency keys, which the plan does not establish; still counts as a delivery attempt in the failure-rate metric.

options.label: C) Accept occasional duplicate emails
options.description: Completeness 2/10. (human: 0 / CC: 0) ✅ No new code. ✅ Window is narrow (marker write must fail right after a successful send). ❌ A stated correctness gap left unhandled and untested; duplicates surface as customer confusion.

answers: A) Skip email if row already has this PI (recommended)

questions.question:
6A — Should automated tests for the handler land in this branch, replacing "None planned"?
Project/branch/task: main, Stripe payment webhook plan (HOLD SCOPE), Section 6 Tests.
ELI10: The plan says no tests, the existing integration suite will catch regressions. That suite has never heard of this handler, so it cannot fail when the handler is wrong. The manual staging replay checks one happy path by hand. Every fix agreed so far (commit before email, named mail rescue, bound-parameter lookup, duplicate-email suppression) is a behavior that only an automated assertion keeps true after the next refactor.
Stakes if we pick wrong: The SQL, email, and duplicate fixes silently regress; the first signal is a customer or an alert storm, not a red build.
Recommendation: A because well-tested code is your stated non-negotiable, the suite is ~15 minutes of CC time, and the staging replay stays as the manual gate it already is.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=1/10
Net: full unit plus integration matrix now, versus happy-path integration only, versus the plan as written.

options.label: A) Full matrix in this branch (recommended)
options.description: Completeness 10/10. (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15min) ✅ Unit tests with a mail double for every named rescue and the ordering assertion; DB-backed integration tests for routing, SQL-metacharacter and Unicode IDs, unknown user, zero orders, one-query orders read, duplicate suppression, and the two-delivery lock schedule. ✅ Red build is the first signal for any regression of 1A/2A/3A/4A. ❌ Concurrency test needs controlled pause/release points to avoid flakiness.

options.label: B) Happy-path integration tests only
options.description: Completeness 6/10. (human: ~2h / CC: ~5min) ✅ Proves routing, lookup, update, and one email end to end. ✅ Small, fast, no doubles. ❌ Leaves the SQL-metacharacter, mail-error, ordering, and duplicate cases unasserted; those are exactly the bugs this review found.

options.label: C) Keep "None planned"
options.description: Completeness 1/10. (human: 0 / CC: 0) ✅ Nothing to write or maintain. ✅ Manual staging replay still runs before broad enablement. ❌ Contradicts the stated engineering preference; regressions in a payment path reach production first.

answers: A) Full matrix in this branch (recommended)
